newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss see 1997 GDP +0.5 pct vs -0.7 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Swiss see 1997 GDP +0.5 pct vs -0.7 pct in 1996.

text.p: Switzerland's official Commission for Economic Policy said it expected the economy to grow by 0.5 percent next year compared to a forecast decline of 0.7 percent in 1996.
The commision said in a statement it expected 1997 GDP to be driven by export growth due to economic recovery in major global markets, especially in Europe, and a weaker Swiss franc.
"However, these positive impulses contrast with declining domestic demand," the commission said.
It said private consumption would remain little changed and public consumption would fall again next year.

"A particular risk for the development of economic growth is posed by potential turbulance in interest rate or currency exchange rates in connection with the uncertainties of European currency union," the commission said.
The commission forecast that unemployment would rise to an annual average rate of 4.75 percent this year and 5.25 percent in 1997.
Both numbers would be records for post-World War Two Switzerland and the highest levels since 4.72 percent in 1994.
The commission listed five main reasons for this year's decline and next year's expected slim growth.
It said damage to Swiss competitiveness from the Swiss franc's strong rise against other currencies in 1994 and 1995 had still not been repaired.
The economy was also burdened by a continuing construction and real estate crisis and by structural changes in major business sectors.
Demand was slowed by continued pressure for deficit reduction in public budgets and in private households.
Finally, the economy was also hit by poor confidence among consumers, employees and some businesses, it said.
The commission, a group of experts which acts as an advisor to the Economics Ministry, listed several recommendations for nurturing growth.
It said economic policy must build confidence and set proper conditions for investment.

"For this purpose, the commision recommends that monetary policy pay appropriate attention to exchange rate and real economic developments," it said in an aside to the independent Swiss National Bank.
"The commission recomends that there be no tightening of monetary policy as long as the real economy shows no signs of improvement," it added.
Other recommendations included continuing a reduction of public budget deficits, but with a stronger focus on preserving investments, and opening the Swiss economy to outside influences.
